questions.question: What is the name of the deepest known point in the world's oceans?
questions.fact: It lies in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, nearly 11 km down. If Everest were placed there, its peak would still be about 2 km underwater.

questions.question: Which is the smallest of the world's oceans?
questions.fact: The Arctic is covered by sea ice for much of the year, and its summer ice has shrunk sharply since satellite records began in 1979.

questions.question: Which body of water is so salty that people float easily on it, at the lowest point on land?
questions.fact: Its shore lies more than 430 m below sea level, and its water is roughly ten times saltier than the ocean.

questions.question: Which warm ocean current helps keep western Europe milder than other places at the same latitude?
questions.fact: The Gulf Stream carries far more water than all the world's rivers put together.

questions.question: What is a giant ocean wave, usually caused by an undersea earthquake, called?
questions.fact: The word is Japanese for "harbour wave". In deep ocean a tsunami can travel as fast as a jet plane, around 800 km/h.

questions.question: What is the periodic warming of the eastern Pacific that changes weather around the world called?
questions.fact: The name, Spanish for "the boy", refers to baby Jesus: Peruvian fishermen noticed the warm water arriving around Christmas.

questions.question: In Spain, what is "calima"?
options: Dust haze blown from the Sahara
questions.fact: Strong episodes can turn the sky orange. In February 2020 a severe calima forced airports in the Canary Islands to close.

questions.question: Which strong easterly wind through the Strait of Gibraltar draws kitesurfers to Tarifa?
questions.fact: Tarifa's other famous wind is the "poniente", a cooler westerly from the Atlantic. Together they make it one of Europe's windiest spots.

questions.question: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels is the main driver of human-caused climate change?
questions.fact: Carbon dioxide in the air has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to over 420 today.

questions.question: Most of the Amazon rainforest lies in which country?
questions.fact: The Amazon river pours out about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers carry into the world's oceans.

questions.question: What is the world's largest desert, if cold deserts count?
questions.fact: Deserts are defined by very little rain or snow, not heat. Antarctica is roughly one and a half times the size of the Sahara.

questions.question: Which desert covers much of Mongolia and northern China?
questions.fact: In the 1920s explorers there found the first nests of dinosaur eggs recognised by science.

questions.question: Which area of Almería is often called Europe's only desert?
questions.fact: Its dry badlands stood in for the Wild West in Sergio Leone's "Dollars" westerns, and old film-set towns still stand there.

questions.question: Which river is traditionally named the world's longest, though some measurements favour the Amazon?
questions.fact: Its two main branches, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, meet at Khartoum in Sudan before flowing on north to Egypt.

questions.question: Which is the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula?
questions.fact: The Tagus (Tajo) runs about 1,000 km from the mountains of Teruel and Cuenca, past Toledo, to the sea at Lisbon.

questions.question: What is the place where a river begins called?
questions.fact: Where it meets the sea is the mouth. If it splits into many channels there, as the Ebro does, it forms a delta.

questions.question: Which volcano erupted on the island of La Palma in 2021?
questions.fact: The eruption, from a new vent later named Tajogaite, lasted 85 days, the longest on record on the island, and buried thousands of buildings.

questions.question: Which national park on Lanzarote is famous for its volcanic "Fire Mountains"?
questions.fact: Eruptions there in the 1730s buried whole villages. The ground is still so hot that a restaurant grills food over a volcanic vent.

questions.question: What is a huge crater formed when a volcano collapses into its emptied magma chamber called?
questions.fact: The word comes from Spanish for "cauldron". Teide on Tenerife rises from inside a giant caldera called Las Cañadas.

questions.question: Which Icelandic volcano disrupted European air travel with its ash cloud in 2010?
questions.fact: Its ash led to the biggest closure of European airspace since World War II, with around 100,000 flights cancelled.

questions.question: The 1883 eruption of which volcano is said to have made the loudest sound in recorded history?
questions.fact: The blast was reportedly heard nearly 4,800 km away on the island of Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean.

questions.question: The "Ring of Fire", full of volcanoes and earthquakes, circles which ocean?
questions.fact: About three quarters of the world's active volcanoes and around 90% of its earthquakes are found along it.

questions.question: Which scale do seismologists now prefer to the Richter scale for big earthquakes?
questions.fact: Each step up means about 32 times more energy released, so a magnitude 8 is about 1,000 times stronger than a 6.

questions.question: In which country was the most powerful earthquake ever recorded, magnitude 9.5, in 1960?
questions.fact: The Valdivia earthquake set off a tsunami that killed people thousands of kilometres away in Hawaii and Japan.

questions.question: Which European capital was largely destroyed by an earthquake, tsunami and fires in 1755?
questions.fact: It struck on All Saints' Day, when many people were in church. It was felt across Spain and helped give birth to modern seismology.

questions.question: What are hurricanes called in the north-west Pacific, near Japan and the Philippines?
questions.fact: In the Indian Ocean and South Pacific the same kind of storm is called a cyclone. Scientists call them all tropical cyclones.

questions.question: What is the calm centre of a hurricane called?
questions.fact: Around the eye is the eyewall, a ring of towering clouds where the strongest winds and heaviest rain are found.

questions.question: What causes the sound of thunder?
questions.fact: Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder and divide by three to get roughly how many km away the storm is.

questions.question: Which instrument measures air pressure?
questions.fact: Evangelista Torricelli, a pupil of Galileo, made the first mercury barometer in 1643. Falling pressure often means bad weather.

questions.question: What is a monsoon?
options: A seasonal wind that brings rain
questions.fact: India's summer monsoon brings around 70 to 80% of the country's yearly rain, so millions of farmers depend on it.

questions.question: What is the vast northern forest of conifers across Russia, Scandinavia and Canada called?
questions.fact: Also called the boreal forest, it is the largest land biome on Earth, stretching right around the top of the globe.

questions.question: Which tree's bark is harvested to make wine corks, especially in Spain and Portugal?
questions.fact: The bark grows back, so trees are stripped only about every nine years. A cork oak can live for over 200 years.

questions.question: What are the oak-studded pastures of western Spain, where Iberian pigs eat acorns, called?
questions.fact: The dehesa is a man-made landscape of holm and cork oaks. Pigs fattened there on acorns give "jamón ibérico de bellota".

questions.question: "Methuselah", one of the oldest known living trees at over 4,800 years, is what kind of tree?
questions.fact: It grows in California's White Mountains, and its exact location is kept secret to protect it from vandals.

questions.question: Which African tree with a huge swollen trunk can store thousands of litres of water?
questions.fact: Some baobabs have been radiocarbon dated at over 2,000 years old, and their fruit pulp is sold as a "superfood" powder.

questions.question: Which plant can grow almost a metre in a single day?
questions.fact: Despite reaching over 20 m tall, bamboo is a grass. Some species flower only once every 60 to 120 years, all at the same time.

questions.question: Apart from one species, cacti are native only to which part of the world?
questions.fact: The prickly pear ("chumbera") so common in southern Spain was brought over from Mexico after Columbus's voyages.

questions.question: Which flower turns to follow the sun across the sky while it is young?
questions.fact: Only young plants track the sun. Mature sunflowers mostly stay facing east, which helps them warm up and attract bees in the morning.

questions.question: Which plant has the world's largest single flower?
questions.fact: Rafflesia flowers can be about 1 m across and smell of rotting meat to attract flies. The plant has no leaves, stems or roots.

questions.question: Which carnivorous plant snaps its leaves shut on insects?
questions.fact: In the wild, the Venus flytrap grows only in a small area of North and South Carolina in the USA.

questions.question: Counting what tells you the age of a tree?
questions.fact: Each ring usually marks one year. Wide rings mean good growing years, so scientists use them to study past climates.

questions.question: Roughly how much of Earth's oxygen is produced by tiny plankton and algae in the oceans?
questions.fact: One tiny ocean microbe, Prochlorococcus, is thought to be the most abundant photosynthesising organism on Earth.

questions.question: What does the Mohs scale measure?
questions.fact: Talc is the softest at 1 and diamond the hardest at 10. A fingernail scores about 2.5, so it can scratch talc and gypsum.

questions.question: Which blue gemstone is made of the same mineral as ruby?
questions.fact: Both are corundum. Red corundum is ruby, and every other colour, even pink or yellow, is sold as sapphire.

questions.question: Which gem is formed inside oysters and mussels?
questions.fact: A pearl forms when the mollusc coats an irritant with layers of nacre. Natural pearls are so rare that almost all sold today are cultured.

questions.question: What is amber?
questions.fact: Insects trapped in amber can be preserved for tens of millions of years. Much of the world's amber comes from the Baltic coast.

questions.question: What is the largest gem-quality diamond ever found?
questions.fact: Found in South Africa in 1905, it was cut into stones for the British Crown Jewels, including the Great Star of Africa in the royal sceptre.

questions.question: What is a geode?
options: A hollow rock lined with crystals
questions.fact: One of the largest known, the Pulpí Geode in Almería, is about 8 m long and lined with giant clear gypsum crystals.

questions.question: Measured from its base on the sea floor, which is the tallest mountain on Earth?
questions.fact: Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises about 10,200 m from the ocean floor, but only around 4,200 m of it is above sea level.

questions.question: In a cave, which formations hang down from the ceiling?
questions.fact: A handy memory trick: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling, stalaGmites grow up from the Ground. When they meet, they form a column.

questions.question: Roughly how much of Earth's fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers?
questions.fact: Antarctica's ice alone would raise world sea levels by about 58 m if it all melted.

questions.question: Roughly how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fact: The oceans hold about 97% of all Earth's water. Only around 3% is fresh, and most of that is locked up in ice.

questions.question: Uluru, in the Australian outback, is a giant what?
questions.fact: It seems to change colour at sunrise and sunset. Climbing it was banned in 2019 out of respect for its Aboriginal owners, the Anangu.

questions.question: What is the green pigment in plants that captures sunlight?
questions.fact: In autumn, trees stop making chlorophyll, revealing the yellow and orange pigments that were in the leaves all along.

questions.question: Which tree is called a "living fossil" because it has barely changed since the age of the dinosaurs?
questions.fact: Several ginkgo trees survived the 1945 atomic bomb in Hiroshima, within about 2 km of the blast, and still grow there today.

questions.question: Jaén province is famous for vast plantations of which tree?
questions.fact: Jaén has over 60 million olive trees, and in a good year it produces more olive oil than the whole of Greece or Italy.

questions.question: Which strange tree of the Canary Islands has red resin called "dragon's blood"?
questions.fact: The famous "Drago Milenario" in Icod de los Vinos, Tenerife, is often said to be 1,000 years old, though experts think it is much younger.

questions.question: Which climate type has hot dry summers and mild wet winters, like most of Spain?
questions.fact: It's also found in California, central Chile, South Africa's Cape and south-west Australia, all of them big wine regions.

questions.question: Which part of the USA is nicknamed "Tornado Alley"?
questions.fact: The USA has more tornadoes than any other country, usually well over 1,000 a year.

questions.question: Around 10,000 to 6,000 years ago, what was much of the Sahara like?
questions.fact: Prehistoric rock art there shows giraffes, hippos and herds of cattle. This "African Humid Period" ended about 5,000 years ago.
